Across 32 in-depth interviews and water-source site visits with women in Gressier, Haiti, fragmented short-term NGO/aid provision, limited state oversight, and a lack of infrastructure records shifted the burden of water access, fees, and repairs onto households and informal local actors. Households attempting to obtain piped yard connections relied on self-financed, informal neighbour-to-neighbour PVC extensions (paying up to the equivalent of US$100 for parts and labour with little recourse when low pressure rendered pipes non-functional), faced erratic valve management, community-wide water shut-offs for non-payment due to unclear bill responsibility, and failed reconnection even after arrears were paid. Residents also faced arbitrary padlocking and gatekeeping by local pump managers and precarious courtesy access to wells and springs on private property, whereas communities with active grassroots water organizations reported shared maintenance, training, and mutual financial support.
